books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

source: original; documents drawn from public-domain sources, paraphrases, and book-grounded data
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Great Depression affected different groups of Americans in different ways from 1929 to 1939.

documents.title: Who lost work first
documents.source: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Depression struck Americans in all walks of life, but not evenly. Women workers were often the first to be fired, in an effort to protect the jobs of male family breadwinners, and minority workers were easy targets for bosses forced to make hard choices. Many men suffered from being unable to support their families, and out of necessity took jobs once reserved for women, minorities, or teenagers.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the Depression's social effects, written long after the events. A summary that compares groups, not a voice from the 1930s.

documents.title: The Scottsboro Boys
documents.source: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9.
documents.text: Paraphrase: In 1931 nine young Black men, the Scottsboro Boys, were accused of raping two white women on a train in Alabama. Despite the lack of evidence, eight were sentenced to death. The American Communist Party organized their defense, and the case drew national attention to racial bias in Southern courts.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the case, written long after the trial. A summary of the verdicts, not a court record.

documents.title: Mexican Americans removed
documents.source: Table built from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9.
documents.text:
| Measure | Number |
| Formally deported by the federal government | Over 80,000 |
| Estimated total removed from the United States | Over 400,000 |
| Share of those removed who were American citizens | Approximately 40 to 60 percent |
documents.sourcing: A table built from a textbook, counting removals rather than arguing a case. Numbers that show citizens were among those forced to leave.

documents.title: Dust Bowl families head west
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9.
documents.text: Paraphrase: From 1934 to 1937, parts of Texas, Oklahoma, and surrounding states were so dry that the region became known as the Dust Bowl, caused by unsustainable over-farming coupled with a devastating drought. Perhaps as many as 400,000 people ended up in California, with about 40 percent settling in the fertile San Joaquin Valley, where many became migrant farmers.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the migration, written long after the events. A summary of the movement, not a migrant's own words.

documents.title: Migrant Mother
documents.source: Dorothea Lange, “Migrant Mother,” Nipomo, California, March 1936. Public domain (U.S. federal government photograph, Farm Security Administration); via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.text: The photograph shows Florence Owens Thompson, a 32-year-old mother of seven and a pea picker, seated with her hand to her chin while two of her children lean against her shoulders, their faces turned away.
documents.sourcing: A photograph taken by a federal agency photographer to show the need for relief. An image meant to move the public, not a neutral record.

documents.title: Farm prices collapse
documents.source: Paraphrase of Princeton Review, Chapter 11, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23.
documents.text: Paraphrase: In rural areas, farmers struggled to survive as produce prices dropped by more than half. Farmers had expanded production during World War I, then faced falling prices, debt, and foreclosure through the 1920s, and the Depression made their position worse.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of farm distress, written long after the events. A summary of prices and debt, not a farmer's own words.

documents.title: The election of 1932
documents.source: Table built from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.9.
documents.text:
| Candidate | Popular vote | Electoral votes |
| Franklin Roosevelt | 57 percent | 472 of 531 |
| Herbert Hoover | 40 percent | 59 |
Hoover won the electoral votes of only six Northeastern states.
documents.sourcing: A table built from a textbook, counting votes rather than arguing a case. Numbers that show how completely voters rejected the incumbent.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Depression affected different groups of Americans in different ways from 1929 to 1939, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of the differences does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the prosperity and limited government of the 1920s, the Progressive era's earlier expansion of federal power, or the Panics of 1893 and 1907.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about how the Depression affected different groups from 1929 to 1939.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about how the Depression affected different groups from 1929 to 1939.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Bonus Army of 1932, Hoovervilles, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, or the election of 1932.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to the Depression with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as Lange photographing for a federal agency, or a textbook account summarizing the Scottsboro case long after the trial.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the differences by showing some hardships crossed group lines, or weighing which groups suffered most and why.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Depression hit nearly all Americans, but it hit them very differently: race, sex, citizenship, and place decided who lost work first, who was pushed out, and who could hope for help.
Context: The 1920s left farmers in debt, wealth piled at the top, and Black and Mexican-American workers already at the edge of the economy, so the crash of 1929 struck a country already divided.
Evidence: Documents 1-2 show the sorting at work: women and minority workers were fired first, and the Scottsboro verdicts show Southern courts judging by race rather than evidence.
Evidence: Documents 3-4 show removal and flight: over 400,000 Mexican Americans were removed, roughly half of them (40 to 60 percent) citizens, while some 400,000 Dust Bowl families headed for California.
Evidence: Documents 5-7 show the human and political result: Lange's photograph puts a face on migrant poverty, farm prices fell by more than half, and voters swept Hoover out by 472 electoral votes to 59.
Beyond the documents: the Bonus Army of 1932 showed unemployed veterans driven from Washington by troops, and Hoovervilles of scrap shacks ringed American cities.
Sourcing: Lange photographed for a federal agency to build support for relief, while the textbook accounts summarize events long after, so each document's purpose shapes what it shows.
Complexity: The differences were real but not absolute: the Depression also crossed group lines, since white-collar professionals lost jobs too, and some hardships, like bank failures, struck savers of every group.
